utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Judge Gwaunza is, for reasons as mentioned in Rule 15 bis, unable to continue sitting in this case, and this will last only during a very short duration, that is, today. And Judge Picard and myself, we have -- we are satisfied that it's in the interests of justice to continue sitting, and therefore we order that the hearing of the case continue in the absence of Judge Gwaunza. We are apparently in private session at this moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we are in open session. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dimitrijevic. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Bakrac will now continue his examination. Mr. Bakrac, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Let us try and look at a video-clip that was not played with the sound yesterday. That is 29D -- 2D977.1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Unfortunately we are attacking with few forces. We are not going to be able to capture all of them. They will all flee to the Borovo [indiscernible]. I will flee there. Some will flee to Vukovar. After that, other forces are doing that, and of course we will find them there. According to that, in the combat, kill everybody. No mercy. They will not show mercy to you. Remember two of our soldiers who were captured alive in Lasovo and mutilated. And think about that the whole time of the combat, meaning it cannot happen again that one of our men is captured. Do you understand? Second thing, to the enemy who is shooting towards you today, show no mercy. This is something that needs to be clear. Those who surrender have to be captured of course."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, what we saw at the end was that those who surrender should be captured. You were in Erdut at the time. Do you know whether there were any prisoners of war, and what happened to them? What was done to them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that there hadn't been any large-scale activities while I was in Erdut. However, there was combat, there were prisoners, and all those prisoners were handed over to the JNA, to the Novi Sad Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any capacities to keep prisoners of war in the training centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have a detention unit. We could not keep any prisoners in the centre. We did not have such accommodation capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have another video-clip and I would then end with that. 2D975.1. This was disclosed by the Prosecutor. The time is 1 hour, 33 minutes, and 31 seconds, to 1.34.24. Mr. Dimitrijevic, while we are waiting for the clip to be played, tell me: Do you know, after the operation in Bijeljina and thereafter in Zvornik, where did the Serb volunteers go to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They returned to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let us look at the video-clip if the booths have had the time to find the transcript. I believe that they are signalling me that they did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And what happened afterwards with your unit? "Well, after that, our unit -- we were stationed in Erdut. We controlled Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. We held those borders. We held that territory. We were a unit for anti-terrorist and anti-sabotage activities, and we apprehended saboteurs who had been infiltrated into Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem from the Ustasha side. I think that we were -- we kept that peace, that semblance of peace, which lasts to this day. Now with UNPROFOR's mediation. But we kept -- then we were the Krajina Police, all of us, because the Vance-Owen Plan came in then and we all joined the Krajina Police. I don't think that we disappointed the people anywhere. We fought like men. And what is most important, we are ready to do that again."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, we have just heard Arkan who says that after Bijeljina they returned to Erdut, and immediately after the Vance-Owen Plan came in they became the Krajina Police. You spoke about registration plates yesterday. When did you receive the Krajina Police registration plates?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. I can't even remember the period. I only know that that was after that political decision and the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. That would have been the beginning or mid-1992, but I'm not sure. In any case, after that document, that international document, was adopted, we applied the instructions from the document and we all became the Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the uniform change as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received blue uniforms that, if not identical, at least they were similar to the uniforms of the Serbian police. They were very similar. I'm not sure about the pattern, but the colour was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say "we received those uniforms." Who from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the TO, from the Territorial Defence. I don't know who issued the order and how, but in any case we all ended up in blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say the TO, do you mean the TO of Slavonia and Baranja?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned the minister of defence yesterday. Did he play a part in the transformation of your troops into the Krajina Police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I suppose that he was the only person who was responsible for that, for the army and the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. They had to start wearing different uniforms, and he was the one who was in charge of implementing that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dimitrijevic. While you were in Zvornik, yesterday you told us that you went there to pick up the bodies of the two fallen soldiers. Do you remember anything that happened on the day when you were there, something out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. As I told you yesterday, I had spent almost an entire day waiting for the transport permit. I had the time to sit down with people and to socialise with them. Something out of the ordinary happened, something that was not common practice, something that was actually strictly forbidden, and that was the receipt of volunteers in a combat area. A person appeared as a volunteer on that very day when I was there, and he conveyed some information to me to the effect that his name was Milorad Ulemek. He came to volunteer as a Serb volunteer guard. He had been captured a day or a couple of days by the Muslims, and then the military leaders from Belgrade intervened and he was released. He came to the JNA. He wanted to join the JNA, but he didn't like it there. He didn't like the attitude they showed towards him, the attitude towards combat. He had different expectations and he had heard stories about how -- some good stories, and later on I had to check all those allegations. And that was the reason why he came to volunteer in the area of combat when we no longer receive volunteers, because we did not have any orders from Arkan to do that. On that day he did not receive weapons. He was not issued with any weapons. He just stayed there for a few hours until we decided what to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you here. When you say "on that day," was that after the end of combat in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was after the end of combat, since I went to pick up the bodies, and that's the day on which all those things took place. It took up some time. I waited on those papers in the municipality. I had this conversation with him. These two bodies were a matter of priority for me. Naturally I had them transported to Belgrade. I took them to Captain Nikolic at the military and medical academy. We had communications in the territory of Serbia. I reported to the commander and said I would check the allegations of the volunteer who had reported in Zvornik. I went to his house, since he gave me his address of residence in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. You tell us a long story in which allegations are mentioned several times, but you have not explained what the allegations were about. What were the allegations brought against Milorad Ulemek? Apparently, because that's what I understand. You have not explained yet what these allegations were. What was he alleged to have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we have misunderstand each other. When I say "allegations" -- well, there was a personal file where he stated, in fact, his name, his address, his date of birth, his educational background, the name of his mother and father. So this was information provided. He stated how he had arrived at that position. So there were these personal details that concerned him. And while I was in Zvornik I checked this information, in fact. I asked him about it. So it was a routine check-up to see whether this individual who had reported to me without any ID was, in fact, the person I was speaking to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- so you checked on the identity of a person, Milorad Ulemek, who arrived as a volunteer and who did not want to join the JNA at this time. Okay, that's -- let's please continue, then. We'll hear what was so special and -- about this event. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 2D981, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Dimitrijevic, what did you do in order to check the information provided by Mr. Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the address provided and determine that he lived there, he was born there. I met his parents there and they confirmed his place and date of birth, and so on and so forth. Certain personal information was confirmed by them, and this showed that the individual who had provided me with this information had been speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What later happened to that individual? Was this individual taken into the guards? Who authorised this and where did he report to if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having checked the information, I informed Zeljko Raznatovic. He said that that was fine. He authorised the entry of this individual into the Serbian Volunteer Guards unit and he went together with the troops to Erdut. That's when the troops left to Zvornik. And soon after, he became a training instructor, given his experience and the fact that he had been a member of the Foreign Legion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, could you please have a look at the personal file. It says the first educational -- or, rather, training centre in Erdut. Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Since I saw this record, after the fall of Vukovar in November no such records were made. We had difficulties when it came to identifying those who had been killed. One of the reasons was that I had a similar personal record while I was in the JNA, and since I had that experience I was able to make such forms for personal records on each and every member.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Milorad Ulemek fill in this kind of record, when you say that he provided information that you went to check?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when I went to Erdut, the information was only on a piece of paper. It was subsequently transformed into a personal record on such a form.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point in time I would request that 2D981 be admitted into evidence. And I failed to ask for 2D977, the previous video-clip, also be admitted into evidence. So that would be 2D977.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect to this document, can we please have information as to provenance. Is this something you obtained from the witness? Or who gave this to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, the witness had this record, brought it with him. The witness had a copy that was left to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour, to that document, then. And with respect to 2D977.1, we request that this be MFI'd along with the other videos that we were MFI-ing from that collection yesterday, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, first the video previously played.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video 2D977.1 will receive number D645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Then what we have on our screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 2D -- document 2D981 will receive number D646, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of position Milorad Ulemek had after he was received and went to Erdut with the SDG? What sort of position did he have and what duties did he perform?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, he went to Erdut as a guard. But given his capabilities and his experience that he demonstrated, he soon became a training instructor and then he made his way up the ranks as the wartime events unfolded. I think his last rank, the highest rank he obtained, was that of lieutenant-colonel or colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, in the course of our conversation you said that during one period of time, from November -- from August to November 1992, you weren't in the party headquarters, you didn't stay there, you were absent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was absent. That was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. "The course of the conversation," are you referring to a proofing or what exactly are you referring to? You said "in the course of our conversation." The question is quite leading. I'd like to know if that came from his testimony; and if so, where? Sorry if I missed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was part of the testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps I leave it to you, Mr. Bakrac, to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- I apologise. I apologise to the booths. Your Honour, when we informed you of the testimony to come, we said that -- when we spoke to Mr. Dimitrijevic, he said he was absent in -- from August to November. And in the course of our proofing here, he gave us the reasons for his absence. Perhaps I should have asked him about this. I'll ask him when he was absent from the Serbian Volunteer Guards in the year 1992 and what were the reasons for his absence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from August onwards, or, rather, from July onwards, but in my case from August onwards, there weren't any wartime activities, no combat, there was no need for my presence, in fact. I asked Zeljko Raznatovic to grant me a leave of absence. I was divorced, but I have a daughter from that first marriage. She was very young and I wanted to spend some time with her, since I had been absent for several months. This leave wasn't limited in time. It was said: When I need you, I'll call you. That's what Arkan said and that's what happened. So this leave of mine was from August until November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And in November 1992, why did Arkan ask you to return?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason was that he had reached an agreement with the people surrounding him, and this agreement was that he should participate in the elections for the republican parliament. He was supposed to be an independent candidate for the Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, Group. So he needed my presence in order to organise these things and everything else that related to this move.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the needs of that campaign at the time, did you engage any volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that was the case at the time. I'm trying to remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After that group of citizens had been formed, did you form a party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But yes only in the extraordinary elections in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the needs of that campaign, did you engage any volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A significant number, in fact. In the party HQ there are about 60 volunteer -- volunteers who performed various kinds of duties there. I can perhaps provide you with the details of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that if necessary. Sir, in October and November 1993, did you pay these volunteers, these employed individuals, in the course of that election campaign? Were they well paid if they were paid at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By definition they were volunteers. They had volunteered to help the party. There were no such obligations. They weren't employed in the sense that they had to be present. If they were present there and performed their duties, it was a matter of their own good will.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Dimitrijevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. And, Mr. Jordash, could you please repeat. You said you would need less time. How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think 45 minutes should do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So just a bit over into the next session. Because we'll -- we have 35 minutes, I think, until ... yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just pick up on some issues which Mr. Bakrac was discussing with you a moment ago, that is, Arkan's reaction to Legija's application to the State Security Service. Did you hear Arkan or were you told by anyone else why it was that Arkan was against that application?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, but I was aware of Arkan's position with this regard. He was against the police, the public police or the secret police. He just didn't like to have anything to do with the police. He didn't want to have any contacts with the police, given his previous experiences from his civilian life. That was part of his character. That was his character trait. Him and Legija were close enough, and my impression that Arkan may have received this as some sort of treason. But he could not keep him because he was of no service to him anymore, there were no war operations undergoing or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just let me understand this, because you've said that he was against the public police and yet he'd interacted with Badza in 1991 without, it seems, any problem; no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a problem, because Badza was there for the same patriotic reasons as Arkan. From the beginning of 1991 to the end of 1991 Badza was the TO commander and thus his immediate superior. So during that period of time there were no misgivings between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Okay. But when did Arkan then develop a problem with the public police? We'll come to the state security in a moment, but when did he develop a problem with the public police, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had not been part of his life then, but it was a notorious fact that he was involved in some incidents in Belgrade, that he had clashes with the security and enforcement forces. He allegedly was -- even did time in prison. Rumour has it that he had hit a policeman. I have no personal knowledge of any of that, but I believe that that was his experience before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to look at the state security. You heard that in 1996 when Arkan -- when Legija was applying to the State Security Service, you heard that Arkan had a problem with the State Security Service; is that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such problems. That -- did I understand you correctly? Your question was about possible Arkan's problems with the state security; is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm trying to focus on why Arkan did not like the idea of Legija applying to join the State Security Service. And I'm interested in, one, how you know that; and two, why that might have been the case. So if you could just focus on that and answer very precisely on those two issues.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, up until the time when Arkan was killed, I was in touch with him. We would see each other. We would have a cup of coffee. Not every day, but we did see each other. And I would often hear him say, "This lad of mine, I lost him to the state security." I interpreted that as him not really being in favour of that. He didn't care much for the fact that Legija had accepted a position in the state security. That's the way I interpreted his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So why do you -- did he say to you or did you learn or infer why it was Arkan did not like Legija joining the State Security Service? What was the problem from Arkan's perspective?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't enter his head, so I really can't interpret the reasons for all that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let's go to a different subject then. Let's take you back in time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, nevertheless -- Witness, you told us, and I quote from your answer: "He was against the police, public police or the secret police." And now asked about why he was against, you say: Well, I couldn't look into his head, et cetera. So that means that you know that he was against the police, including the secret police, but you've got no idea why. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1991. I want to have you have a look at a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P404, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is an interview rather than a speech, an interview given by Radmilo Bogdanovic in 1993. Whilst that's coming on the screen, do you know who Bogdanovic, Radmilo Bogdanovic, was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you know about his connection to Red Star in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a time even when he was the honorary president of the football team and he was on the management board of the Red Star football team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at the time he was on the management board, was Arkan connected to Red Star?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the leader of the team's supporters, the supporters of the biggest football team in Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that they became friends, Arkan and Bogdanovic, in 1991 as a result of or as a consequence of their relationship with Red Star?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At the time, they were in close contact with each other in relation to Crvena Zvijezda issues, as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to the football-supporting or football supporters' issues; is that right? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because controlling football fans was one of Arkan's main obligations. I was also a fan, you must understand, so I was familiar with that period in his life. I was a Delije fan in the northern part of the football stadium. So controlling discipline, making sure that the fans acted correctly, and so on and so forth, these were things for which Arkan was responsible. So all of us who went there to watch football matches knew very well how things were organised and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and what the hierarchy was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did some of Arkan's men, the men who came as recruits to the training base in Erdut, did they come in part from this supporters' group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That was a basic cell, so to speak, from which the Serbian Volunteer Guards was developed. 15 or 20 lads were from the northern part of the Crvena Zvijezda stadium and they moved over to join the Serbian Volunteer Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know if you'll know this or not, but feel free to say if you don't; was Bogdanovic as a member of the management of that football club in some way also -- in some way a member of the management of the football supporters' group as well? Was that the nature of the relationship between Bogdanovic and the management board and the football-supporting group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. That was perhaps something that occurred within the framework of Crvena Zvijezda, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's have a look at what Bogdanovic said and see if you can confirm or not what he had to say about the origins of the Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. And it's 27 at the bottom right-hand page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I'm interested in this paragraph, where Bogdanovic says: "As I know in my capacity of the President of the Board for the Serbs outside of Serbia, Arkan assembled 250 to 300 volunteers - do not quote me on the number - I told him to report to General Simovic, i.e., the minister of defence, which is where he, as the volunteer, really reported --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that the B/C/S version hasn't been shown to the witness. What Mr. Jordash is reading out is not on the screen in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any way to get to the right page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I thought it was on page 27 of this magazine. It is the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's the subtitle on the right-hand side of the page towards the top which is -- starts off with "Uloga MUP ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, it's the paragraph where Bogdanovic is talking about being approached by Arkan, and Bogdanovic telling Arkan to report to General Simovic, the minister of defence. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't got it in front of me. I'm looking at the wrong part of the article. I'm trying to find the relevant paragraph in the Serbian, but I can't see very clearly. It's -- the letters are small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, even without knowing one word of that language, it's somewhere that "250 to 300" should appear. Now you are pertinent that it was that portion you drew our attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go up the page, please. I do apologise. Can we zoom out again, please. It's below the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's below the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at the top right column, the part that we were just focusing on. It's there. It's just not in digits, it's in words. The numbers are in words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have it now, Mr. Witness? I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know about this arrangement or this occurrence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Erdut at the time, when this arrived, but I went to see the agreement implemented because I know that we contacted General Simovic with regard to our ammunition needs, weapons needs. We even contacted the general when we had to take care of those who had been killed and wounded. So at the beginning, towards the end of November and in December we had contact on the basis of a recommendation Bogdanovic told Arkan, as far as I can understand, to report to General Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you told that at the time or soon thereafter when you joined Arkan's men, were you told that Bogdanovic had this relationship with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary for them to tell me about this. I knew about this before the war. He didn't go to Zvijezda during the period of the Serbian Volunteer Guards. He went there a lot earlier. So all of us who were fans of the Crvena Zvijezda knew that Bogdanovic was part of the management of the Crvena Zvijezda football club because he was on good terms with Arkan when it came to issues concerning control of the fan club.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But did you know that Bogdanovic had told Arkan to go and see Simovic, and Arkan had taken that advice?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I wasn't present. But I personally contacted the General Staff and the general in order to request assistance that was needed in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Arkan boast about his relationship with Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct that Arkan would go and see Simovic on a regular basis in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general, yes. He would see General Simovic; as to how regularly, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But from where you were working, Arkan obtained his supplies through his relationship with General Simovic and his relationship with the JNA. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I have just said. That was the only way, the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. "That was the only way"? Is --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only way for us to have the needs satisfied, the needs that the Serbian Volunteer Guards had for weapons, when it mentions 250 or 300 volunteers here in the article. But I'd like to say that Arkan would always increase the number so that he could ask for more equipment and then he'd get what he would get. So that was his idea when he requested assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Arkan would obtain more weapons and more supplies than he actually needed by telling JNA representatives and General Simovic that he had more men than in fact he actually had; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to say. Because he wasn't sure that they would give him everything he had asked for. So he thought: I'll ask for more; and if we receive less, that will be fine too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the training base at Erdut. Were you in a position to see for the whole of -- well, from the time you joined in November of 1991 through 1992 how this training base operated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash perhaps before we -- the witness answered this question could I ask you one. Did you ever attend any of the meetings Arkan had with General Simovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that when Arkan asked for the equipment for the men Bogdanovic refers to in this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't present when they negotiated, tried to reach an agreement for the first time. I was present on the occasion of a different meeting, when Arkan asked for the army to make it possible for him to increase the number of vehicles they had. We were to receive some vehicles, jeeps, and so on and so forth, so that it would be easier to move around the front line in Slavonia and Baranja. General Simovic didn't authorise this request, and he was quite angry and nervous because of this. Because in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem it was difficult for us to communicate and to -- with the -- or to have contact with the vehicles that we had at our disposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I asked the last two questions because it's -- may be important for the Chamber to find out exactly what is knowledge or facts and what is interpretation of attitudes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was the meeting, approximately, you attended, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when I arrived in Belgrade, at the end of February and the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was present at the meeting besides -- if anyone, besides you, Simovic, and Arkan?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two other JNA officers. Apart from Arkan and myself, there was Marko Pejic, as far as I can remember, and another member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm after an impression; what was your impression of the relationship between Arkan and Simovic during that meeting? Did they appear to know each other well and like and -- and like each other?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was well received. They had a good discussion. The end of the discussion was satisfactory, but Arkan wasn't happy because the army wasn't in a position to comply with his request for those vehicles at the time. So the meeting wasn't a successful one. But in spite of that fact we were well liked by General Simovic and we continued to co-operate with him when it came to receiving weapons and ammunition. He was in contact with the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, Biorcevic, as well. So the army did have a means of communication that was somewhat different from the means of communication that we were used to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why did Simovic refuse that request for vehicles? Do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason was that he didn't have the means of complying with the request at the time. There were many wartime events, and he wasn't in a position to comply with the request, because he didn't have that number of vehicles available, the number of vehicles that Arkan had requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that despite the refusal on this occasion by Simovic, that the co-operation continued and the co-operation was good. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I co-operated directly with the army. There were certificates that I issued to members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards so that they could deal with their health problems, needs when it came to weapons. I also dealt with the platoons that were present at burials. So we had various forms of communication mainly with the army. And if General Simovic hadn't been favourable, he would have probably reacted in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So through 1992 you saw weapons and supplies coming into Arkan's camp directly from the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And no one else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. And no one else ... there were others. There was the command of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you see weapons and supplies coming into Arkan's camp in 1992 from anyone or any organisation other than the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that yesterday. We were on good terms with the army. We sent requests to address either to the command of the TO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or the Ministry of Defence of that entity. Or we sent requests to General Biorcevic, the command of the Novi Sad Corps. These are the only two addresses we used when we requested weapons, ammunition, bombs, grenades, Zoljas, Osas, whatever the warehouse needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I note the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Jordash, of course, this is the kind of confusion the Chamber wants to avoid. Your question was about what came in, and the answer was about whom they addressed with requests, which is not the same. Now, even if you look at the questions about what came in, there may be some confusion as well. "Did you see weapons and supplies coming in" directly from the military? The answer was yes. No one else? No one else. And then we developed that. Of course, we should keep in mind that analytically there are two possibilities, that he saw everything coming in and knows all of that what the source was; the second option is that he had not seen everything coming in. And it might be difficult to know whether you have seen everything, yes or no, because if you have missed something, you may be aware that you missed something, but you also may be unaware that you missed something - you just have not observed that. That's the kind of questions which are not resolved by your questions and answers, apart from that your last question was about what came in and the answer was not about what came in, but what was requested. I'm just pointing this to you so that you are better aware that an analytical approach of questions and answers leaves quite a bit of questions open. I'm not saying that at the end if you would have dealt with it systematically that they would not still be open, but at least it has not been fully explored. I just want to make you aware of how the members of the Chamber -- the Judges in the Chamber are used to analyse questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I thought I was approaching it systematically, but I'll do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of my observations if you still take that position then I might have to review my analysis. But let's not enter into that debate at this moment and rather take a break. How much time would you need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think 15 minutes should -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 1.00 and then you have another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the next 15 minutes are yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were in charge of logistics at the Erdut camp in 1991. Did that mean all weapons and ammunition would at some point come through you? All weapons and ammunition that was coming to the camp would come through you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the paperwork. We had a depot. We had a man who was responsible for the depot. When the equipment arrived, he would send me the papers, the paperwork, to file.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did the paperwork consist of?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "paperwork," I mean a document that lists what was delivered, from whom, who received the delivered goods, who confirmed the receipt of the goods. I kept the archives. I maintained the situation of the stock in the depots. So if anybody asked me at any point in time, I had a record of the stock currently held in the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So there's no one from that camp who would have had a better understanding or better knowledge of who was providing supplies to the camp; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nobody knew better. However, the person who was in charge of the depot was also aware of the current situation of the stock in the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And it's right, isn't it, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question there. The paperwork and the actual situation are two different matters. Would you have the full certainty that whatever arrived in the depot was always accompanied by paperwork that reached your desk? Could there ever be any discrepancy between the actual situation in the depots or even within the centre but outside the depots and what was on your desk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Such an error could not have occurred. As we read the morning order, we were told exactly what was being done in Erdut. For example, if one part of the unit was on target practice, the person in charge of the depot was supposed to provide all the necessary ammunition, and that information was also provided to me. So I had daily insight into the situation at the depot. As needed, I would be provided with the information on the goods coming into the depot, and every day I would deduct those things that were taken out of the depot, because every day there was either an action, operation, target practice. There was something going on every day, and the ammo was issued from the depot every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you go to the depot yourself to verify whether what you received on paper was in every respect in accordance with what was in the depot? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I went to the depot every day and I compared the situation on paper with the situation in the depot. The person who was responsible was a man who provided me with the exact information on the current stock. Any error, any mistake, would have been punishable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, punishable or not -- again, you apparently did not check it yourself, physically, to say: On my list I see 247 hand-grenades. Where are they? Let's count them. That's not what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. That would have been too much. And the quantities were huge. It would have been impossible to take the physical stock of all the ordnance day-in/day-out. But we knew approximately -- or not approximately, actually we knew the exact number of crates, the quantity of ordnance, the number of reserve rifles, the number of hand-grenades, Zoljas, Osas. It was impossible to have any discrepancies, either surpluses, however minor, or any minuses, again however minor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there any possibility that, in the centre or perhaps even outside the centre, that stock was there which would not have been accounted for in the paperwork?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There was no such thing. We had a depot, one depot. We had one person in charge of the stock. He had perhaps four or six volunteers under him because his job was demanding. That was the part of the unit that he was in charge of, and there was just one depot, one place, that received all the ordnance and weapons and from which all the ordnance and weapons were issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you're telling is that you were not aware of any other stock outside of the depots because, according to your knowledge, there was only one depot which contained all the ordnance and weapons. That's how I have to understand your answer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only that I didn't know; there was no other depot save for the one that I was aware of. Yes, you understood my answer absolutely correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the person in charge of the stock, can you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, the person was Borivoje Ackov [phoen], also known as Bore Ackov.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there was a discrepancy when weapons came in or ammunition came in, for example, between what was expected or what was on the paperwork as compared to what physically arrived, was there any obligation on his part to react to that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in his job description. For example, if one part of the unit was on a combat mission, a lot more ammunition was given to them. On their return from the operation it was hard to just guess how many rounds were fired. He had to take the reminder back from the troops, enter that quantity into the depot books, and copy me with the new situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But what -- let me give you a hypothetical. Biorcevic delivers or says he's going to deliver 20 AK-47s. The paperwork arrives. It says "20," but only ten arrive. Would he have an obligation to react to that; and if so, how would he be expected to react?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, such things absolutely didn't happen. We're talking about weapons in a combat area. Every bullet, every rifle was taken stock of. There were no such errors, either in the JNA or in the Erdut centre, especially when it comes to rifles and bombs. Our accounting was very pedantic. And if there was -- if there should have been such a case, he should have reacted accordingly. But such things didn't happen. And second of all, we didn't have AK-47s. We had M-70s, but I'm talking about rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... and is it the case that if something like that happened he would have been expected to report it to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was his obligation. But I never encountered such a problem during my tour of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me stop you, because I'm running out of time. But am I correct that you never saw any deliveries of weapons or ammunition from the Serbian DB during your time in 1991 and 1992 at Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. And I know that things like that didn't happen later either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I also right that you do not know Mr. Stanisic? You have no relationship with him professionally or personally. You never have had, have you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your statement. I've not seen Mr. Stanisic before. This is the first time ever I see Mr. Stanisic. In person, I mean. I saw him on TV and in newspapers of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you've never spoken to him before?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's the same for Simatovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the same for Simatovic. I had an occasion to meet him sometime in 1996 or perhaps the beginning of 1997. Milorad Lukovic - and I already told you that we shared a property of Zombie disco club - called me. He was out of Belgrade and he told me that a colleague of his, a very important person in his job, would be a guest in our disco club. He wanted me to act as a very hospitable host to him, and I was. And that was that one occasion when I actually met Mr. Simatovic. He was with a large crowd of people on the time -- on that occasion when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now just very quickly now. Training, how many people do you think were trained in the Erdut centre in 1991 and 1992? Are you able to give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in 1991 and 1992, we're also talking about one part of 1993 and one -- and 1994. About three -- 3500 to 4000 people were trained there during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 3.500 to 4.000 people over 1991, 1992, and 1993. And am I correct that this, again, had nothing to do with the DB of Serbia as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 1994 and even one part of 1995 there were no contacts. There was no communication with regard to equipment, training, or any such thing with the state security or whatever you called that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There's been evidence in this case, Mr. Witness, that there was a training base at Fruska Gora in 1991 where 50 people were trained over a period of five months. Did your training camp, training this number of people, have anything to do with that training camp?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of any such thing. This was not part of the Serbian Volunteer Guards or otherwise I would have known about that, but I don't. This is the first time ever I hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take you back to Simovic if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, please P1050.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something that Simovic's secretary, a woman called Glisic, said. I want to ask you about a comment she made in her diary about Simovic and see if you can comment on it and perhaps shed some further light on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have page 10 of the English and 14 of the B/C/S. And in terms of the book, you're looking for page 59 of the book. Page 9 -- sorry, page -- let's go over to page 10 of the English and B/C/S page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Glisic is writing about the relationship between Arkan and Simovic. And if we go to the bottom of the page in the English, where it says: "Arkan's mischief often made us laugh." If you find that in the B/C/S. And then we'll read on about what Glisic says about a particular TV programme that Arkan appeared on. "Studio B ... was broadcasting a talk about the establishment of a Serbian army. Our General Simovic was to take part together with volunteers from the front. Everything had been arranged in advance with the editor, and Simovic decided to go on air with all of them, to go public and speak about the establishment of a Serbian army, about the need for an organisation of volunteers, about their courage. He wanted to say in public that they enjoyed his support, support of the minister of defence. But just before the broadcast the minister was 'prevented and otherwise occupied.' Somebody was against his going public, although it had been announced that he would take part." Just reading on, just to cut out some time, I'm interested particularly in this bit: "We all froze when the moderator asked --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the witness does not have the right page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he had before on all parts that Mr. Jordash read, and I now asked, for the last part, to move to the next page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "We all froze when the moderator asked Arkan in public who was his Commander-in-Chief. "There was silence in the office and we all expected Arkan to speak after a short silence and say right there in public 'General Simovic.' "Patriarch Pavle! "Everybody laughed. It was not serious, it was just his way."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of this TV programme? Were you aware of this idea amongst the Ministry of Defence that Arkan regarded Simovic as his boss?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this show, I'm afraid. I'm not aware of the reasons why this show was aired. But I believe this is a good illustration of the relationship between Arkan and General Simovic. It was a close relationship, as you can see, and it was mutually benevolent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And finally, we spoke a moment ago about Legija, and Arkan being upset with Legija about Legija's application to join the State Security Service of Serbia in 1996. Am I correct that -- I know you don't know the reason why Arkan was upset about that, but can we take from what you observed and what you heard and what you saw that you never, throughout your whole time with the Tigers, perceived the Serbian DB to have any special relationship with Arkan, is that a fair -- or any relationship with Arkan from what you saw. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Ms. Marcus, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: According to your evidence, you joined the SDG in November of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you did not have any affiliation with Arkan or the SDG prior to November 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You were not an associate of Arkan's prior to November 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Following your deployment to Erdut, you returned to Belgrade at the end of February or the beginning of March of 1992, where you operated as the chief logistics specialist in the SDG headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You testified that between August and November 1992 you were on leave spending time with your daughter. Now, from November 1992 until March 1993 you worked for the Party of Serbian Unity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: But in March 1993 Arkan sent you to Pristina, in Kosovo, to manage the football club there. Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you volunteer for that or did Arkan send you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job, which provided me with my livelihood before the war, was to work at the representative office of the Novo Mesto-based Krka. However, my favourite pastime was football because before the war I used to play football, and all that came into the equation leading to my departure for Pristina. And I'm still very much involved with football, even today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you only worked for five months at the party headquarters and then you were sent to Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I returned from my leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: According to the information we have from the Defence, you were in Pristina only for three or four months, and that was from March to June 1993. What did you do between June 1993 and March 1994 when you were injured in the traffic accident?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I reiterate that this is information that we received from the Defence team. My question was that you were in Pristina then for only three months, from March till June of 1993. And my question was: What were you doing between June 1993 and March 1994, when you were in a traffic accident?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the end of that year's championship, which was in June, the stint with the Pristina football club was over and I returned to the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guards. My three-month-long absence when I was in Pristina was not a permanent affair. I would be in Pristina for three days and the rest of the week I would be in Belgrade. So it was not a stay in continuity. It was a temporary stay in Pristina. I shared my time between Pristina and Belgrade, so I never interrupted any of my ties with Belgrade. Because the -- my job managing the football club in Pristina was not a full-time affair. I had to attend games and trainings. But I continued communicating with Belgrade very closely. When the championship was over, I returned from Pristina, I returned to Belgrade, and I continued to work as if that short stint had not even happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, I encourage you to try to answer my questions as briefly as possible. If I would like further clarification or if the Chamber would like so, we will certainly ask you for that. Thank you. You testified that in November 1991 you tried to sign up for the JNA but you were rejected due to your age. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Then, as an alternative, the JNA suggested that you go and volunteer with the SDG; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The JNA did not tell you that signing up with the SDG would be another way, actually, to be signing up with the JNA, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me that. And I didn't even think about that, to be frank. When I spoke to an official from my municipality, I was rejected. The person said, "You're too old, this will last for some time, stay at home." I didn't want to. I said, "Where should I go, then?" He said, "Well, go to see Arkan. You'll have order, work, and discipline there if that is where you want to go."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you signed up with Arkan's SDG, did they not issue you papers on behalf of or as an organ of the JNA, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no papers of any kind initially when I arrived, not only for me but that was also the case for all other volunteers who had registered. Everything was a matter of volunteering. But after a while this changed. The reason for the change is that individual combatants or volunteers would arrive for two or three days. They'd be there for two or three days or a week, they wouldn't be happy with the conditions, and they would leave the Serbian Volunteer Guards. And as a result it wasn't possible for Arkan to have a trained unit that could operate in the battle-field. So the HQ of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, we decided that all volunteers who came and reported should first sign a certificate stating that they would stay there for a minimum period of one month.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what you testified to previously. So prior to your arrival and your setting up of the paperwork, there was no paperwork associated with the SDG volunteers. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 90 per cent of the cases, yes, I came across some papers but they hadn't been skillfully compiled, not in accordance with the professional norms. So I tried to rectify the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You said yesterday at temporary transcript pages 20 to 21 that your impression was that the SDG was a very serious organisation. And you testified at that same transcript page that the training centre had a military postal code. I have attained your military records from the Serbian Ministry of Defence, and I do not see any entries in your military records indicating that you had any connection with the JNA in 1991 in Erdut. During your time with Arkan's SDG in Erdut in 1991, were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were the Serbian Volunteer Guards attached to the TO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and as such we co-operated with the JNA on the battle-field. We acted together. So I didn't say that we were part of the army or that we had been recorded as part of the army. We were the TO, the 101st Training Centre in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srijem. I think I explained that yesterday, and I'm repeating it today. We were, quite simply, on very good terms with the JNA when we contacted it in order to obtain various forms of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, just for the record, your reference to yesterday's page is now 16.059.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm afraid that's going to be a repeating problem because as of the last break I didn't see the permanent transcript page numbers in my e-court. I'm sorry. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'll do my best -- obviously for tomorrow I'll be ready with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have it on my screen now and often it changes during our next-day hearing. So it's just to make life easier for those who come in after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting. If Ms. Marcus wants to continue with her examination with regard to the issue of military participation, I would like her to show this extract from the military records that she has referred to if she has it on her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm happy to call it up, or I can simply send it to the Simatovic Defence. I wasn't planning on tendering it. It's a response to an RFA that we got last week. I can send it to you if you want and -- unless the Chamber would like me to show it. That was my last question on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, I think if you first send it to Mr. Bakrac, and then we'll see whether at any later point in time -- although apparently relevant for this witness, I wonder whether it had -- had not yet been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to be fair, we have received it. But if my colleague would like to use this document, I thought it might be good to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But apparently Ms. Marcus sees no reason to do that. Of course in the re-examination or further cross everybody can proceed as it deems fit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't intend to tender it, but it's available, as we said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, just so that I'm sure to understand what you said: Your evidence is that the relationship between the SDG and the JNA was, quote, and I'm quoting from today's transcript, page 70, line 6: "Quite simply, on very good terms with the JNA when we contacted it in order to obtain various forms of assistance." Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence correctly that Arkan's SDG moved about the SBWS without any registration plates on their vehicles, crossed back and forth between the Serbian border with no registration plates but only with SDG emblems on the vehicles between November 1991 and the end of February 1992 while you were stationed in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, could Ms. Marcus tell us where exactly the witness said that they would cross over into Serbia in those vehicles without registration plates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not exactly what Ms. Marcus put to the witness. At the same time, Ms. Marcus, it would be wise that if you asked the witness to confirm your correct understanding of the evidence, that you do not move away from it too much. So as far as border crossing is concerned, if you could give us the relevant -- the licence plates are clear, I think. Two Pajero jeeps, one --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I have to agree with Mr. Bakrac. The witness did describe some Sombor licence plates and some registration plates. And Mr. Bakrac is correct and I apologise for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I still have page 54, yes, that he asked about the border crossings and it was not the ones with just the stickers. So I do apologise to everyone for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in order to move around the SBWS - I'm leaving out the border part now - with vehicles that just had stickers and no registration plates on them, the SDG must have had the highest level of authorisation from the SBWS authorities in order to secure such freedom of movement; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You testified that the SDG "enjoyed the support of all the institutions in the field. When I say that, I mean the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem region as well as the military structures, and I mean the JNA." Now testified about the proximity of the SBWS government to the Erdut SDG training centre and that government representatives would visit the training centre regularly. Is this your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm just going to put a few more selections to you and then ask you a series of questions about that. You testified that you had "contact in particular with the Territorial Defence command in Western Srem. We would list our needs, and I personally would take that list to Dalj, which is where I would hand over the list of our needs for that day." And you added: "We were members of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem." You also testified that Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza, was the TO commander and that he was in the training centre at least five to six times per month. This is your evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I refer the Chamber in relation to this to Exhibit P494, page 5; and evidence on the 8th of December, 2010, at transcript page 10030.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, you testified, therefore, that Goran Hadzic was president of the SBWS government at the time you were there, in the fall of 1991, and that he visited and even stayed in the SDG training centre on a regular almost daily basis. In order to achieve such close co-operation, there were regular meetings between Arkan, Badza, Hadzic, and the military leadership in the SBWS. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I please refer the Chamber to Exhibit P494, pages 5 and 6; as well as the transcript dated 27th of May, 2010, at page 5447.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution, for tomorrow, to give us a list of these transcript references, because tomorrow if we have to examine after the witness -- after the Prosecution, it would be -- expedite things I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The military leadership who you said were having regular meetings with Arkan, Badza, and Hadzic, included Ilija Kojic as minister of defence of SBWS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you are aware that he was the one who appointed Mrgud as deputy minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I refer the Chamber to Exhibits P16 and P1678.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware, then, at the time that Badza was in charge of the SBWS TO, he was employed by the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I thought he was from the surroundings, since he often appeared and would meet those people whom I saw on a daily basis. So I thought that he was from the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So I suppose you were also not aware that at the same time Ilija Kojic served as minister of defence for SBWS, that he was officially employed by the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I refer the Chamber to Exhibits P325 and P1628.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So your evidence is that Arkan and his SDG were in regular communication with and co-ordination with Hadzic, Badza, and Kojic so that all the forces in the area would be working together toward the same goals. Would that be according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wouldn't include Kojic. At those meetings I mostly saw Mrgud Milovanovic a lot more than him. I wasn't present at their meetings when they tried to reach agreements, so I don't know what they agreed on. But that was basically the circle of individuals who, during that period of time, took decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You have explained to us your role as the logistics co-ordinator both in Erdut and later at the SDG headquarters in Belgrade. You must have kept very careful records - in fact, you explained how carefully you kept those records - of the logistics operations to ensure that the books were kept carefully. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did all I could to perform my duties to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Where are those records kept today?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you keep any of those records yourself for your own personal archive?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And this personal file that I have provided to the Defence was a file I had on me by chance. I didn't keep anything else and I didn't have the desire to keep anything on me, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you left the SDG, according to the Defence that was in 1996, where were the archives and all the documents stored at the time that you last saw them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
