utterances.text: In the party HQ. Or, rather, of the Serbian Volunteer Guards Lugice Pravde [as interpreted] 1 is the address.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: During the time that you were in charge of logistics in Belgrade in 1992, Vlado Vukotic was in charge of logistics at the SDG training base in Erdut; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was in 1993. He was a volunteer from Belgrade. We know each other, but I think that was later. It wasn't when I left. He wasn't even in Erdut at the time that I was there. He arrived a lot later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In his previous answer, the address the witness mentioned was "Ljutice Bogdana."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So in 1992, when you were in Belgrade, who was the corresponding logistics co-ordinate at the SDG centre in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have anyone in particular. Various individuals succeeded each other to perform these duties, and they were designated as the centre commander. There wasn't anyone who did the same sort of work as I did. I covered a variety of duties in the centre, and this was then broken down into three or four directions. So there were several individuals who concerned themselves with these things. They had a centre commander. Predrag Bojovic was there immediately after I left for Belgrade, and I handed over some of my duties. He was a lieutenant-colonel. He was a volunteer from the very first days when the Serbian Volunteer Guards was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So in 1992 you were actually operating in both Belgrade and Erdut. Do we understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Belgrade. But there were normal communications, because everything that was needed was sent from Belgrade to Erdut. So there was very close communication and it was necessary for there to be such communication, for everything to function smoothly. From Belgrade I communicated with people in Erdut and dealt with the problems that arose in the course of the day, if there were any such problems, of course. But, as I say, there wasn't just one person who was responsible for all those duties, for all the logistics in Erdut who replaced me. I had to deal with three or four individuals who had shared the duties I previously performed in Erdut. So some of them were responsible for volunteers. One of them was responsible for the warehouse. Another was responsible for the food. There was one responsible for car repairs, for everything that had to do with mechanical needs. So these individuals were responsible for these things and I communicated with them from Belgrade, and this all depended on what was needed at the time. But there wasn't just one individual who performed all these duties. While I was there, however, I did everything myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You testified that you were informed a day before the Bijeljina operation of the number of men who were to be involved in that operation. So you were involved, then, in the logistical preparation for the Bijeljina operation; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a certain extent. Yesterday I said that Arkan was very proud of the fact that Biljana Plavsic had invited him to participate in this action, and he made this known in front of a number of us who were present at the time. And I was immediately given the task of compiling a list of individuals who would be in a certain sense both in Belgrade and in Erdut. This was done to have a record in case anyone was wounded or killed, and we needed to have such records in both places.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just so that I understand your answer: You said you were given the task of compiling a list of individuals who would be in a certain sense both in Belgrade and in Erdut. Do you mean the list of individuals who participated in the Bijeljina operation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were the preparations for the Bijeljina operation done in secret?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they weren't. But no one walked the streets crying out about this. It was within the framework of Erdut, the Serbian Volunteers Guard. I received information about the 60 [Realtime transcript read in error "16"] individuals who were supposed to participate. No one told us about how confidential our role and task was to be, if that's what you had in mind. Perhaps the army insisted on such things, but I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could we seek clarification. Did you talk about 16 or 60 individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 60, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Marcus, I need three minutes at the end of this session. Could you find a moment somewhere in the next two or three minutes to conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, just with one more question it would be best then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you in Bijeljina before, during, or after that operation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think I'll pause there for the day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Dimitrijevic, we'll conclude for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the morning. Ms. Marcus, could you give us an indication already as the time you'd need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask for the full time which we noticed which was three hours. I've probably used about 45 minutes. So with your leave I would -- I would use the two hours and 15 minutes approximately that remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll see whether there's any chance that we could conclude your testimony tomorrow. We'll try to do our utmost best and so will the parties too. I again instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in any way about your testimony, whether testimony you gave yesterday and today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. I further remind you of the other instructions I gave to you earlier this morning. Then could the usher escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could just inform the Chamber of one thing while the witness is going out. This was in response to Mr. Bakrac's question about Exhibit 2D901. We have not tendered that. There was e-mail communication from us on the 16th of November, 2011, and we repeated our position in court on the 21st of November, 2011, at page 15037, generally that our position is that we oppose document -- redacted documents being admitted but in this particular instance, due to the specific contents and the redactions that are contained therein, we do not oppose its admission, so -- in redacted form, if the Chamber sees fit. So we said we did not have any position against admission, but we didn't actually tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I could correct my earlier mistake now. Perhaps this should be evidence that is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about numbers and sources which I not immediately can match with. Is there anything at this moment, Mr. Bakrac, you think we should do in order to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There's a name here. I'm not sure whether one can conclude that it concerns the witness, that it relates to the witness, but there is the name of the protected witness there, and that is why I think that this should perhaps be a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But has it been tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It has not been tendered -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it has not been tendered, then of course confidentiality -- I mean, the Chamber can rule on protective measures for exhibits that are admitted into evidence. I do see that it is D647 apparently -- oh, that is the number that has been reserved for it. Yes, so it's not yet tendered, but we have reserved the number for it. I leave it to the parties whether they want to tender it, yes or no. But the document itself needs --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggested that it should be admitted into evidence, but Ms. Marcus wanted some time to state her position with regard to the allegations. I think she has now said that she isn't against it, but I suggest that it be filed as a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We do not oppose admission. We do agree that it should be under seal. And we request that the Simatovic Defence provide a full translation, because it hasn't been translated yet. But we are familiar with it and we do not oppose admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then pending a complete translation, D647 is now marked for identification. And once the translation is there, the full translation, it will be admitted. That having said, the Chamber still needs an update for the witness we discussed yesterday. I don't know how confidential details are. I also do not know, but it's the witness who was hospitalised and couldn't travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday we were late coming out of the courtroom. We tried to get the witness on the phone. We tried again this morning. My team has been tasked with checking on the situation, and we can inform you in writing to update you on the witness situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if there's anything -- I mean, we're talking about a witness who was supposed to appear next. So no problem if you send us an e-mail. But do you say: "I have no further information at this very moment"? Then we'll wait for your e-mail messages this afternoon. If, however, you have any information, please share it with the Prosecution and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let me tell you that if the witness is not able to come, we can call DFS-009 next week, because obviously we won't have the time to do it this week. So our next witness D FS-009 can be called to come in next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it from your answer, where you say "if the witness is not able to come," that you do not know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. If -- if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then the brief answer to my question whether you have any information. Apparently you have no such information which allows you to say anything about whether he will be able to come. I think we yesterday invited the parties to further see how to use the coming days as efficiently as possible. The Chamber would like to be informed about it, if possible, this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you that the Prosecution's position hasn't changed. But I have spoken with Mr. Jordash and the witness that we talked about has testified several times. We do not know whether he speaks English, so it likely is that he's going to have to sit down and listen to audio tapes of the six or so trials that he testified in. So I think it's probably not possible for that witness to achieve all of that before next week. The Prosecution will be prepared to cross-examine the next witness. It is very challenging and we may come to the Chamber seeking some additional time if we are unable to complete our preparations, but we will work towards that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber staff -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- the Chamber staff is instructed to communicate with the parties this afternoon to see where we are and what exactly is within the possibilities and what is not within the possibilities. I would rather not spend further time on it at this moment in court, unless there is a matter which you say we should know before we adjourn. There is not. Then we adjourn. And we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 19th of January, 9.00, in this same courtroom, II.
